details:
**Slaying Medusa**
Perseus's most famous feat was beheading Medusa, the only mortal of the three Gorgons (her immortal sisters were Stheno and Euryale), whose gaze turned people to stone. He avoided her gaze by looking only at her reflection in a polished shield. He then escaped the pursuing sisters while invisible, and later gave the head to Athena, who placed it on her aegis.

**Killing Acrisius with a discus**
An oracle told King Acrisius of Argos that his daughter's son would kill him. Years later, while competing in funeral games held by King Teutamides of Larissa, Perseus threw a discus (or quoit) that the wind carried astray. It struck and killed Acrisius, fulfilling the prophecy by accident.

**Danae and the shower of gold**
To keep the prophecy from coming true, Acrisius locked his daughter Danae in a bronze chamber or tower. Zeus reached her in the form of a shower of golden rain and fathered Perseus.

**Cast out to sea in a chest and rescued by Dictys on Seriphos**
After Perseus was born, Acrisius locked Danae and the baby in a wooden chest and threw it into the sea. It washed up on the island of Seriphos, where the kindly fisherman Dictys took them in and raised Perseus. After returning, Perseus made Dictys king of Seriphos.

**Polydectes and the bride-gift**
Dictys's brother Polydectes, king of Seriphos, wanted to marry Danae and wanted Perseus out of the way. When each guest brought a horse as a gift (supposedly for the bride-price of Hippodamia), Perseus had no horse and rashly offered anything else, so Polydectes demanded Medusa's head. When Perseus returned, he turned Polydectes and his court to stone with the head.

**Gifts from the gods: winged sandals, cap of invisibility, shield, kibisis, and harpe**
Perseus was equipped by several gods and nymphs. Hermes gave him winged sandals and an adamantine sickle (harpe), and Athena gave him a polished bronze shield. Hades's helmet (cap) of invisibility and a magic bag (kibisis) that expanded to hold the head came from the nymphs (Hesperides) in some accounts, from the gods in others.

**The Graeae and their shared eye**
The Graeae (Gray Sisters) were three ancient sisters of the Gorgons who shared a single eye and a single tooth. Perseus grabbed the eye as they passed it between them and held it hostage until they told him the way to the nymphs who held the magic items and to the Gorgons' lair.

**Rescuing Andromeda from Cetus**
On his way home, Perseus came upon the Ethiopian princess Andromeda, daughter of King Cepheus and Queen Cassiopeia. She had been chained to a rock as a sacrifice to the sea monster Cetus because Cassiopeia boasted that she (or her daughter) was more beautiful than the Nereids. Perseus killed the monster and married Andromeda.

**Phineus and the wedding fight**
Andromeda had earlier been promised to Phineus, Cepheus's brother. Phineus (sometimes paired with Agenor) and his followers attacked Perseus at the wedding feast, and Perseus turned them to stone with Medusa's head. This Phineus is not the blind seer met by the Argonauts.

**Pegasus and Chrysaor**
When Perseus cut off Medusa's head, the winged horse Pegasus and the warrior Chrysaor, her children by Poseidon, sprang from her neck. Pegasus was later tamed by the hero Bellerophon.

**Turning Atlas to stone**
When the Titan Atlas refused Perseus hospitality, fearing that a son of Zeus would steal his golden apples, Perseus showed him Medusa's head and turned him into the Atlas Mountains of North Africa.

**Founding Mycenae and the Cyclopean walls**
Perseus founded Mycenae, by legend at a spot where the cap (mykes) of his scabbard fell off or where he found a mushroom (also mykes) that held water to quench his thirst. Its massive walls were said to have been built by the Cyclopes, which gave the name "Cyclopean masonry."

**Trading kingdoms with Megapenthes**
Ashamed of having killed his grandfather, Perseus did not take the throne of Argos. He traded it to his cousin Megapenthes, son of Proetus (Acrisius's brother, whom Perseus killed in some versions), for Tiryns. In one account Megapenthes later killed Perseus.

**Snakes of Libya**
As Perseus flew over Libya carrying Medusa's head, drops of her blood fell to the sand and became venomous snakes. One of them later killed the Argonaut seer Mopsus.

**Descendants: Electryon, Alcmene, and Heracles**
Perseus and Andromeda's sons included Electryon and Sthenelus. Electryon's daughter Alcmene was Heracles's mother, making Heracles Perseus's great-grandson, and Sthenelus was the father of Eurystheus, who assigned Heracles his labors.
